L0@P0: Treatment Of Metastic Osteosarcoma
L1@P0: Osteosarcoma (OS) is the most common malignant bone tumour in children and teenagers.Osteosarcoma
L2@P0: is also the most common bone tumour in dogs, accounting for 90% of all bone tumours in this species.
L3@P0: The major complication of OS is the spread (metastasis) of the tumour from the bone to the lungs In
L4@P0: spite of chemotherapy, human patients who develop metastasis have a very poor prognosis with a 5-year
L5@P0: survival rate of less than 20%. In dogs, 90% will develop pulmonary metastasis, and in spite of
L6@P0: treatment, less than 20% will be alive 2 years after diagnosis. Metastasis thus remains the most
L7@P0: significant and untreatable complication of both human and canine OS. It is clear that in order to have
L8@P0: any chance of long-term survival, these patients will require treatment with novel and targeted biological
L9@P0: therapies.
L10@P0: Using a series of cutting-edge technologies that have allowed us to look at genetic and
L11@P0: molecular changes in osteosarcoma tumour cells, participating centres have identified a
L12@P0: new molecule called thioredoxin reductase (TrxR), which contributes to OS metastasis.
L13@P0: Auranofin is an inhibitor of TrxR. Auranofin is used in humans and in dogs for the
L14@P0: treatment of active, progressive, or destructive forms of inflammatory arthritis, such as
L15@P0: rheumatoid arthritis. We now have preliminary data in a mouse model of OS showing that
L16@P0: auranofin dramatically reduces OS lung metastasis. Therefore, auranofin has clinical
L17@P0: potential for the prevention/treatment of both human and canine OS metastasis
L18@P0: In this study, we are testing auranofin for its ability to inhibit lung metastasis andincrease survival in
L19@P0: dogs with OS. If successful, this study will result in near-term veterinary and human patient benefit. It will
L20@P0: change veterinary practice for the treatment of OS, and pave the way for clinical trials in human patients
L21@P0: Expected Risks: Auranofin is used to treat some forms of arthritis in humans, dogs and cats. At high
L22@P0: doses, auranofin causes some gastrointestinal disturbances (e.g. diarrhoea), but this problem is generally
L23@P0: resolved by lowering the dose. This trial will begin with a lower dose (3 mg tablet every 3 days) than the
L24@P0: maximum recommended dose in dogs (9 mg daily), so it is expected that side effects will be avoided. Rare
L25@P0: side effects of auranofin use can include reduced numbers of platelets, red blood cells or white blood cells.
L26@P0: In addition, auranofin may lead to kidney, liver or skin complications. However, these side effects are rare
L27@P0: and all dogs will be monitored throughout the trial, and the dose lowered or discontinued if adverse side
L28@P0: effects are observed.
L29@P0: Expected Benefits: Auranofin has been tested in a mouse model of OS and was effective at significantly
L30@P0: reducing lung metastasis without any side effects. We expect that auranofin will not decrease survival in
L31@P0: dogs but that it will reduce metastasis in a similar manner as in mice, and that as a result, it may increase
L32@P0: disease-free survival of canine OS patients. In addition, pre-clinical data gathered from this study will be
L33@P0: critical for follow-up in human patients, where the potential exists for auranofin to also decrease
L34@P0: metastasis and increase survival. Significantly, this trial may lead to new management practice in canine
L35@P0: OS patients.
L36@P0: Participating Centres:
L37@P0: (1) Sarcoma Research Group, The University of Queensland Diamantina Institute, Brisbane, Qld.
L38@P0: (2) The Australian Animal Cancer Foundation, Brisbane Veterinary Specialist Centre, Brisbane, Qld.
L39@P0: (3) Department of Orthopaedics,The Wesley Hospital, Brisbane, Qld.
